opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting and underappreciated questions in the economics of AI.

Right now, most pricing is basically per token. You pay roughly the same whether the model is writing a limerick or helping figure out why a drug candidate is failing in trials. That's a bit strange when you think about it, because the value of those outputs differs by many orders of magnitude. A token is a token from a compute standpoint, but it's not a token from an economic standpoint.

Early in a technology's life, cost-based pricing makes sense. It's simple, it's legible, and customers are still figuring out what the thing is good for. But as models get more capable, and especially as they move from answering questions to doing extended, agentic work, like running for hours, writing and testing code, doing research, the gap between what it costs to produce the output and what the output is worth gets enormous. I'd expect pricing to drift toward reflecting that, at least in some segments.

You might see a few things happen. One is more tiering by capability: the frontier model that can solve the hard problem commands a real premium, while more routine tasks get commoditized and pushed down toward marginal cost. Competition will do a lot of that. If several providers can all summarize an email well, that price goes to near zero. The premium survives only where you're doing something others can't.

Another is more outcome-based or task-based pricing. Instead of "here's your bill for 40 million tokens," it's closer to "this agent resolved this many support tickets" or "this completed this engineering task." That's more natural for enterprises, because they think in terms of labor and outcomes, not tokens. It's harder to implement, though. You have to define what success means, and you have to trust the measurement.

I'd also add a caution. I don't think it's healthy for the whole value of AI to be captured by whoever sells the model. A lot of the benefit should flow to the users, the businesses, and society more broadly, through things like faster science, better medicine, and cheaper services. Competition between labs helps with that, and I think that's actually good. The way I'd frame it is that pricing will become more differentiated, but the overall trend is that the cost of a given level of intelligence keeps falling dramatically, even as the frontier stuff stays expensive because it's doing things that were previously impossible.

So in short: less uniform per-token pricing, more segmentation by how hard and valuable the task is, and a growing split between commoditized intelligence and frontier capability.

r001.rationale: It says a token has the same compute cost but can differ in economic value by many orders of magnitude depending on the task.

r002.rationale: It predicts outcome-based pricing, such as charging for support tickets resolved or engineering tasks completed.

r003.rationale: It mentions agents running for hours, but does not suggest charging based on time worked or an hourly rate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underappreciated questions in the whole industry, because right now we have this very strange situation where the pricing is basically uniform. You pay per token. And the token that helps a high school student write an essay costs about the same as the token that helps a biotech company figure out which compound to synthesize next. And those two things obviously have wildly different economic value. Orders of magnitude different.

So the current model is almost like if electricity were priced the same whether you were running a nightlight or an aluminum smelter. Actually, that's a bad analogy, because electricity is kind of priced that way and it works, because electricity is a commodity and the value is captured downstream. The question is whether AI is going to be like that, or whether it's going to be more like, say, consulting or legal services, where the price tracks the value to the customer rather than the cost to produce.

My guess is it bifurcates. For a lot of use cases, the token-based pricing will persist and the price will keep falling, because there's competition and the marginal cost really is low. That's the commodity layer. But I think increasingly you'll see pricing that's tied to outcomes. If a model does the work of a junior analyst, or a software engineer, or eventually a researcher, the natural way to price it is in terms of what that labor would have cost, or what the output is worth, not how many tokens got generated. We're already seeing hints of this with agents. When the thing runs for six hours and comes back with a finished piece of work, nobody really cares about the token count. They care whether the work got done.

The thing that makes this tricky, and I say this as someone who runs a company that has to make these decisions, is that the models that are capable of the high-value tasks are also the ones that are capable of the low-value tasks. It's the same model. So you can't easily segment by capability the way you might in other industries. You end up segmenting by context, by what the model's being used for, by the reliability guarantees, by the integration. And that's a bit awkward, because it's not how we've traditionally priced software.

There's also a dynamic where the frontier is where the value is, and the frontier is expensive to produce. Training these models costs billions. So there's a very real question of whether the value gets captured by the people building the models, or whether it's competed away and flows to the users. I honestly think a lot of it will flow to the users, which I think is actually a good outcome for the world, but it does create a tension in terms of funding the next generation of models, which is where the safety work also has to happen.

So I don't have a clean answer. I think the honest answer is it's going to be messy for a while, and the pricing models will lag the actual economic reality by a few years, as they usually do.

r001.rationale: It contrasts tokens used for a student essay and biotech research, saying their economic values differ by orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It predicts pricing tied to outcomes and says customers will care whether the work gets done.

r003.rationale: It mentions pricing based on what comparable labor would cost, but does not say AI services may be paid for by time worked or hourly.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tension between the cost of producing an output and the value that output creates. You could spend the same amount of compute writing a birthday card as you do answering a question that saves a company a million dollars. So the economic value can vary enormously, even when the underlying cost is similar.

But that doesn’t mean you can charge the second customer a million dollars. If another company can provide the same answer, competition is going to push the price down. The important question is how differentiated the models are, and whether the provider can reliably deliver an outcome that others can’t.

I’d expect a mixture of pricing models. Charging for tokens makes sense when you’re providing a general-purpose input and the customer is building something on top of it. As systems take on more complete tasks, charging per task—or perhaps based on a measurable outcome—could make more sense. But then you have to establish what counts as success and how much of the result was actually attributable to the AI.

So I don’t think there’s one pricing model that wins everywhere. It depends on how easily you can measure the value, how reliable the system is, and how much competition there is for that particular task.

r001.rationale: It says economic value can vary enormously for outputs using similar compute, contrasting a birthday card with an answer that saves a company $1 million.

r002.rationale: It says pricing could be based on a measurable outcome, which communicates payment tied to results.

r003.rationale: It discusses token, task, and outcome pricing, but does not suggest charging for time worked or hourly labor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between what it costs to produce an answer and what that answer is worth. You might use the same amount of computation to write a birthday message and to help solve a problem that’s worth a million dollars to a company. The economic value is very different, even if the cost of serving the model is similar.

Today, pricing is mostly tied to usage—how many tokens you consume, how much computation you use. As models become capable of doing longer, more substantial tasks, I’d expect a wider range of pricing models. You could imagine paying for a completed task, or for a service that comes with some assurance about the quality of the result.

But capturing a fraction of the value is harder than it sounds. How do you measure the model’s contribution? How do you distinguish a valuable discovery from an answer that looked promising but went nowhere? And if several companies can provide comparable intelligence, competition will put pressure on prices regardless of how valuable the output is.

So I’d expect a mixture. There will be relatively inexpensive, broadly available intelligence, and there may be more expensive services where you’re paying for reliability, specialized capabilities, or the ability to carry a difficult task through to completion.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a birthday message with help on a million-dollar problem, explaining that outputs can have very different economic value despite similar serving costs.

r002.rationale: It predicts customers could pay for a completed task, making payment depend on task completion rather than token or compute usage.

r003.rationale: It mentions pricing by tokens or computation, but does not suggest charging for time worked like hourly labor.
